https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw99.text: Image source, Vincenzo Nuzzolese/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images By Davide Ghiglione in Rome Published 1 hour ago The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class. A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate". Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year. Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality. "You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition. There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear. The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible. The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf. The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through. Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU. The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently. In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school. In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system. Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching. The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained. The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered. The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days. Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law. The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools. Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank. The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren. Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge. "We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said. Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago. The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government". Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/02/us-s.text: The nail-biter poll is being "very closely" watched by US President Donald Trump, who has championed Latin America's swing to the right in recent elections.Washington suspended consular services in Brasilia over "security concerns," and Australia closed its embassy for the same reason. Neither gave details.Pressure from Trump has loomed large over a campaign dominated by scandals and insults that has done little to ease Brazil's deep political polarization.Edinho Silva, president of Lula's Workers' Party (PT), told journalists that the US closing its consulates "makes absolutely no sense. It is one of the ways Trump has to vie for Brazilian public opinion."Veteran leftist Lula, 80, is in a dead heat with the son of far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, and opinion polls predict the vote will go to a runoff on 25 October."The race is tied but not at a standstill," said Felipe Nunes, director of the Quaest polling institute.Many of the nation's 160 million registered voters are disenchanted with their options.Marcelo Vilanova, a 32-year-old fish market manager in the southeastern city of Juiz de Fora, said he was voting for Lula as the "lesser of two evils."Lucas Sales, 38, a cell phone shop owner in the city, is voting for Flavio Bolsonaro even if "he himself isn't the best option," citing his promise to be tough on crime — a key concern for many Brazilians in this election.'Turned into a circus'The scramble for undecided voters has had both sides on alert for anything they can twist to their advantage.In recent days, Brazil's patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, became the focus as rumours erupted that Flavio Bolsonaro planned to strip her of her position if elected.Bolsonaro, 45, issued fierce denials as Lula took to the campaign trail clutching a statue of the beloved saint, declaring that "messing" with her was "unacceptable."The electoral court ordered Thursday that posts with the "untrue" claims be taken down.Next, Bolsonaro and his supporters pounced when Lula said that men were "cowards" when it comes to getting their prostates examined, while "women learn to receive a touch from a young age," referring to gynecological exams.Clips of his comment circulated widely on social media as if it were an allusion to abuse."It's really turned into a circus," said Gisele Sousa, 45, a clothing shop employee. "My vote won't go to any of them."In another jab during a podcast on Thursday, Lula said he was sure he would win in the first round, over a rival he said was not even qualified "to serve as a building manager."A tough foeLula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, boasting he is fitter than ever despite his advanced age.He made Brazilian sovereignty a central plank of his campaign, warning Trump not to "meddle" in his country's elections.The former union leader has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment while massively curbing deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.Nevertheless, voters complain about the high cost of living and are fed up with violence and crime.Lula unveiled a flurry of measures in the election run-up to win over voters, increasing social welfare payments and banning sports betting that has ensnared many in gambling addiction.Bolsonaro was also confident of a first-round win, vowing that Lula would be "ousted from the presidency" on Sunday."Brazil can't stand you anymore," he said.The once little-known Bolsonaro, a senator since 2019, has proven a tough foe for Lula, even as it emerged that he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic "Dark Horse" about his father.He was forced during the campaign to admit he had asked jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro, at the heart of one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases, to bankroll the film.

https://www.politico.eu/article/burnham-.text: LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated Monday his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament. Asked by ITV's Good Morning Britain Monday whether he wanted to rejoin the EU, Burnham said: “I'm going to be honest and say, in my lifetime, I would like to see that happen but I am not going to move ahead of the public. “I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the public, the British public, are the bosses.” Advertisement Advertisement At the ruling Labour Party's conference last month, Burnham called for closer links with the EU. He has yet to spell out precise details of the relationship he would seek — but the party's 2024 election-winning manifesto under Keir Starmer ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union or accepting freedom of movement with the bloc. Burnham said Monday that the promises of the 2016 referendum that took Britain out of the EU have not been delivered. “We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign,” he said. “It's weakened our economy. It's also weakened our control of immigration and that might surprise people.” But he said: “I'm not proposing rejoining in this Parliament. We're way, way away from that at this particular moment in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better than the arrangement we've got right now.” The PM's remarks come after he told the Sunday Times that accepting freedom of movement with the bloc should not be off the table in future negotiations. A U.K.-EU summit is scheduled for next month, although that is set to focus tightly on technical tweaks to the existing relationship rather than addressing bigger questions of Britain's future ties to the bloc.
